facts.fact_text: A G8 summit of Heads of State and Government was held from 6 to 8 June 2007 in Heiligendamm, in the vicinity of Rostock.
The police estimated that there would be around 25,000 participants at an international demonstration in Rostock on 2 June 2007.
The police estimated that there would be around 15,000 demonstrators present during the G8 summit in Heiligendamm.
In June 2007 the applicants drove to Rostock in order to participate in demonstrations against the G8 summit in Heiligendamm.
The applicants were arrested on 3 June 2007 following the identity check and search of the van in front of Waldeck prison.

On 4 June 2007 at 4.20 a.m. the Rostock District Court, having examined the first applicant in person, ordered the first applicant's detention (amtlicher Gewahrsam) until 9 June 2007, 12 noon at the latest.

On 4 June 2007 at 4 a.m. the Rostock District Court, having examined the second applicant in person, ordered the second applicant's detention (amtlicher Gewahrsam) until 9 June 2007, 12 noon at the latest.
On 9 June 2007 at 12 noon the applicants were released from prison.
The Rostock District Court relied on section 55(1), paragraph 2(a), of the Mecklenburg-West Pomerania Public Security and Order Act (the PSOA) in ordering the applicants' detention.
The Rostock District Court relied on section 56(5) of the Mecklenburg-West Pomerania Public Security and Order Act (the PSOA) in ordering the applicants' detention.

Section 55(1), paragraph 2, of the Mecklenburg-West Pomerania Public Security and Order Act (the PSOA) provides that a person may be detained if this is indispensable in order to prevent the imminent commission or continuation of a criminal offence.

Under section 55(1), paragraph 2(a), of the Mecklenburg-West Pomerania Public Security and Order Act (the PSOA), the assumption that a person will commit or aid and abet a criminal offence may be based on the fact that he or she has announced or incited the commission of the offence or carries banners or other items containing such incitement.

Under section 55(1), paragraph 2(c), of the Mecklenburg-West Pomerania Public Security and Order Act (the PSOA), the assumption that a person will commit or aid and abet a criminal offence may be based on the fact that he or she has been apprehended in the past on comparable grounds as a person involved in the commission of offences, and if facts warrant the conclusion that a repetition of this conduct is to be expected.

Section 56(5) of the Mecklenburg-West Pomerania Public Security and Order Act (the PSOA) provides that if the police take a person into custody, they must immediately obtain a judicial decision on the lawfulness and continuation of the detention.

Section 56(5) of the Mecklenburg-West Pomerania Public Security and Order Act (the PSOA) provides that the judicial decision must set a maximum duration of detention, which may not exceed ten days in cases governed by section 55(1), paragraph 2.
The police considered that there was a threat of terrorist attacks during the G8 summit in Heiligendamm.
Having regard to the experience of previous G8 summits, the police considered that there was a risk of property damage by left-wing extremists during the G8 summit in Heiligendamm.
The police estimated that approximately 2,500 of the 25,000 participants at the international demonstration in Rostock on 2 June 2007 were ready to use violence.
The police estimated that approximately 1,500 of the 15,000 demonstrators present during the G8 summit would be ready to use violence.
On 2 June 2007 serious riots broke out in Rostock city centre.
400 policemen were injured during the riots in Rostock city centre on 2 June 2007.
The Rostock District Court found that the applicants' detention had been lawful in order to prevent the imminent commission or continuation of a criminal offence.
The Rostock Court of Appeal found that the applicants' arrest and continued detention was indispensable in order to avert a danger to public security and order.
On 3 June 2007 at around 10.15 p.m. the applicants' identity was checked and established by the police in a car park in front of Waldeck prison.
At the time of the identity check on 3 June 2007, the applicants were standing next to a van in the company of seven other people in the car park in front of Waldeck prison.
The police searched the van in the car park in front of Waldeck prison on 3 June 2007 and found folded-up banners bearing the inscription 'Freedom for all prisoners'.
The police searched the van in the car park in front of Waldeck prison on 3 June 2007 and found folded-up banners bearing the inscription 'Free all now'.

The Rostock District Court found that, as the applicants had been found in front of Waldeck prison in a van in which objects calling for the liberation of prisoners had been discovered, it had to be assumed that they had been about to commit or aid and abet a criminal offence.

The Rostock Regional Court found that, as the applicants had been found in the vicinity of Waldeck prison in possession of banners with an imperative wording ('free'), they had intended to incite others to free prisoners, which constituted an offence.

In their further appeals before the Rostock Court of Appeal, the applicants, represented by counsel, submitted that the slogans on the banners had been addressed to the police and the authorities, urging them to end the numerous arrests and detentions of demonstrators.

In their further appeals before the Rostock Court of Appeal, the applicants submitted that the slogans on the banners had not been meant to call upon others to attack prisons and to free prisoners by force.

In their further appeals before the Rostock Court of Appeal, the applicants submitted that the interpretation that the banners called for attacking prisons and freeing prisoners by force had to be considered far-fetched, given that there had not been any violent liberation of detainees from German prisons in recent decades.

The Rostock Court of Appeal found that the banner 'Free all now', together with the banner 'Freedom for all prisoners', could be understood as an incitement to liberate prisoners, an offence under Article 120 of the German Criminal Code.
The Rostock Court of Appeal found that the police had been entitled to assume that the applicants had intended to drive to Rostock and display the banners at the partly violent demonstrations there.

The Rostock Court of Appeal found that displaying the banners at the partly violent demonstrations in Rostock might have incited a crowd ready to use violence to liberate people who had been arrested and detained.
The Rostock Court of Appeal accepted that the slogans on the banners could be understood in different ways.

The Rostock Court of Appeal found that in the tense situation in and around Rostock the police had been authorised to prevent ambiguous declarations which could have led to a risk to public security and order.
The Rostock Court of Appeal found that the duration of the applicants' detention was proportionate.

Both applicants argued before the Federal Constitutional Court that it had been far-fetched to interpret the slogans on the banners as inciting other demonstrators to attack prisons and to liberate prisoners.

The applicants submitted before the Federal Constitutional Court that the banners had been addressed to the police, who had already arrested many anti-globalisation activists, to the participants in the G8 summit and to the public in general, and had not advocated acts of violence.
No criminal proceedings were brought against the applicants for having incited others to free prisoners.

Under section 52 of the Mecklenburg-West Pomerania Public Security and Order Act (the PSOA), the authorities may order a person to leave a place or prohibit a person from going to a specific place (Platzverweisung) in order to avert a real danger.

Under section 52 of the Mecklenburg-West Pomerania Public Security and Order Act (the PSOA), if the facts warrant the conclusion that a person will commit an offence in a specific area, the person may be prohibited from entering that area for up to ten weeks.

Under section 61(1), paragraph 1, of the Mecklenburg-West Pomerania Public Security and Order Act (the PSOA), an item may only be seized in order to avert an imminent danger to public security or order.

Under section 61(1), paragraph 4, of the Mecklenburg-West Pomerania Public Security and Order Act (the PSOA), an item may only be seized if the facts warrant the conclusion that it might be used in order to commit a criminal or regulatory offence.
